PRESCHOOL · AGE 3 · CLASS 7

Body Parts & My Five Senses

Age 3 YearsClass Preschool 7Subjects Body parts & the five senses

Twenty-four cards about the one thing your child knows best: their own body. Meet your head, your hands and your wiggly fingers, meet the five senses that explore the world, point, find and match — this class follows Animals & Their Sounds on the preschool path.

Body-part words are words your child uses all day long: hands for clapping, feet for stomping, ears for listening. You say the word, your child points to it — that is the whole lesson, and it never feels like one.

Start Today’s Class ↓Grown-up nearby, little one wriggling like a finger — both work.
TODAY’S CLASS

How today’s class works.

Five little steps, in any order that suits you: a welcome from your teacher, the body-part cards, the five senses, solving the body sheets together, off-screen play, and a warm goodbye. Stop after any step — that is a complete class, and there is never a score at the end.

TEACHER WELCOME

“Hello, my friend — and hello to you, grown-up helper! Today’s class is all about YOU: your head, your wiggly fingers, your stomping feet — and the five amazing senses that help you explore the whole world. Hands on your head — let’s go!”

— Your Kiddo School teacher

Fifteen parts, one amazing kid.

Say it, then show it

  • The pair is the whole game: “hands!” — then clap, clap. “feet!” — then stomp, stomp. Every body part gets a word and an action.

Five ways to know the world.

Eyes see, ears hear, the nose smells, the tongue tastes, the skin touches — five senses, always working together. Read each card slowly, then try the little experiment it offers.

The five senses, in one breath

SOLVE THE SHEETS — ON PAPER OR ON SCREEN

Solve the body sheets together.

The twenty-four body and sense cards print two to a page, straight from your browser. Printed, cut and named, they are the class’s real worksheets — and on screen, every card page can be drawn on directly.

  1. 01

    Print the cards

    Open the printable cards and print all twenty-four, two to a page. Cut them out together, naming each body part as it is cut.

  2. 02

    Point to your own

    Hold up a card — head, chin, knee — and point to that part on your own body. The word lands where the part lives.

  3. 03

    Try the senses

    On the sense cards — see, hear, smell, taste, touch — try each sense out loud: what can you hear right now? One sense a day is a lovely pace.

  4. 04

    Trace the body

    On paper, trace your child’s hand on the back of a card and label the fingers together. On screen, the card page’s Write & Color layer is the crayon.

Open the printable cards ↗Draw on the cards on screen ↗

Every card page has a Write & Color layer: your child can draw right on the card with a finger, a stylus or the mouse, then save the finished work. Nothing is uploaded anywhere.

OFF-SCREEN PLAY

Your body, live from your living room.

Body parts and senses are made for away-from-screen play: no toys needed, and the star of the show is standing right in front of you. Pick one of these — two minutes is plenty.

Simon says, Kiddo edition

  • “Simon says touch your nose! Simon says clap your hands! Stomp your feet!” — leaving Simon out now and then is the best part, and getting caught means a giggle, not a loss.

A quiet listening minute

  • Sit together, close your eyes and count the sounds you can hear: a car, a bird, the fridge, a footstep. Ears on, voices off — five seconds to start, longer if it catches on.

A looking walk

  • On the way anywhere, be sense detectives: find something red, something tiny, something high up, something that smells interesting. Every find gets its sense word said out loud.

The feel basket

  • Collect three things that feel different — a soft blanket, a smooth spoon, a bumpy sponge. Touch each one and say the word: soft, smooth, bumpy. Eyes closed doubles the fun.

One safety word for this class: hands, ears and noses explore everything, but mouths only taste real food that a grown-up has checked — never anything found on the ground or handed over by curiosity.

A NOTE FROM THE PRINCIPAL

For the grown-ups.

Body-part words are the beginning of three big things: self-care (hands wash, feet get socks), safety (a child who can say where it hurts is easier to help) and science (the five senses are the first scientific instruments anyone owns). None of this needs a lesson plan — naming body parts while dressing, bathing and walking does the whole job. When your child points and names, answer with the word and one more: “Yes — and what do your ears do?”

TIPS FOR PARENTS

How to use this class.

Say the word and point to it — the pair is what sticks. “Head!” while you pat your head teaches faster than any worksheet, because your child’s own body is the picture book. Let your child take the taps in every game, even when the answer looks obvious to you: the finger teaches the mind.

Then flip the game: your child says the word and YOU point. Getting one wrong on purpose — patting your elbow when they say chin — keeps the game alive for weeks, and being the caller is powerful practice for a three-year-old.

Age 3 is a guide, not a deadline. If today’s class was two round cheeks and one loud stomp, today’s class was a success.

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · BODY PARTS & FIVE SENSES FLASHCARDS · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Head — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson starts at the very top. The head is the body part your child has known longest — it shook no before any words arrived — and naming it properly opens the whole map of the face and the five senses living on it.

    What is this?

    The head is the top part of the body: a round home for the face, the brain inside and all the sense organs — eyes, ears, nose and mouth. Everything your child uses to see, hear, smell, taste and talk is gathered in this one place.

    What does it mean?

    The head sits on top for a reason: it is the body’s lookout tower. High up, the eyes see further, the ears catch more, and the brain inside gets first news of everything. Your child’s head also does the showing — nodding yes, shaking no, tilting to listen — before any words are needed.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs to know: the head is the body part on top, it holds the face and the brain, hats and hoods and hairbrushes all live on it, and it moves in useful ways — nodding for yes, shaking for no, tilting when something is interesting.

    Why this matters

    Body-part naming is the first map a child ever learns, and the head is its capital. A child who can name the head and everything on it can follow directions, describe aches and feelings, and take part in the games — heads up, head down — that preschool runs all day.

    What it teaches

    Body-part vocabulary and body schema (the internal map of self), imitation and motor control in the nod-and-shake games, the five-sense organs as a set, and self-identity — my head, my face, my smile.

    Words to learn

    headfacebrainnodshaketop

    Say this to your child

    “"This is your head — the very top of you! Your head holds your face, your eyes, your ears, your nose and your mouth, and your brain works inside it all day. Nod your head: yes! Shake your head: no! Your head talks before your mouth does."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and ask what body part this is — the smiling boy’s face with dark hair makes the answer easy. Then point to the word: head.
    2. Find your child’s head with both hands: round on top, face at the front, hair up top. Name each neighbour — eyes, ears, nose, mouth — as you touch near it.
    3. Play the head-moves game: nod your head yes, shake your head no, tilt it slowly side to side like you are listening. Your child copies each one.
    4. Name what lives on the head: a hat goes here, a hood goes here, the hairbrush visits every morning. Head as a place, not just a part.
    5. Finish with the lookout tower idea: the head sits on top so the eyes can see far and the ears can hear wide. Ask your child to look left, look right, from their tower.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look at the picture together: whose face is this — a smiling boy’s? What color is his hair? Which word sits under his face? What is your own head doing right now?

    Ask your child

    "What is the top part of your body called?" "What does your head carry — name them all!" "How does your head say yes? And no?" "What do we put on our heads when it is cold?"

    What your child can say or do

    Your child may nod and shake through every question for a day, name the whole face-country map — eyes here, ears here, nose here — or report proudly that the brain lives inside and it is thinking right now.

    Out in the real world

    Heads are named all day long: heads up at crossing the street, brush your hair, hat on for the cold, chin up at the doctor’s. Every one of those daily phrases lands better on a child who knows exactly which part the word means.

    Try it together

    Follow-my-head: you move only your head — nod, shake, tilt, look up, peek down — and your child copies like a mirror. Swap roles. Add slow-motion mode and robot mode. It is imitation, motor control and connection in one seated game.

    Understanding check

    Ask: "What is this body part? What does your head carry? Show me yes and no with your head." The name, the list and the nod — that is the lesson landed.

    Parent tips

    Touch is what makes body maps stick — name each part while your hand is on it, not from across the room. And let the head be silly sometimes: a head that can tilt like a curious bird or droop like a sleepy puppy is a head fully explored.

    This lesson pairs with the Head flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Body Parts & Five Senses Flashcards.

    Eyes — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson meets the busiest pair on the whole body. Your child’s eyes have been working since before birth — watching, finding, reading the world — and now they get their name, their games and their care rules.

    What is this?

    Eyes are the two seeing parts of the body, sitting side by side in the face. They take in light and turn it into pictures inside your head — the dog in the garden, the page in the book, the face across the table. They work in a team: both eyes look at the same thing at once.

    What does it mean?

    Seeing feels effortless, which is exactly why it hides its own magic: light comes in, and pictures get made. The eyes also guard themselves — blinking spreads a tiny wash of tears that keeps them clean and comfortable, hundreds of times a day without anyone deciding to.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs to know: eyes are for seeing, they come as a pair and work together, they blink all by themselves to stay wet and clean, and they are precious — no poking, no rubbing when hands are dirty, and no looking straight at the sun, ever.

    Why this matters

    The eyes carry most of the information a preschooler learns from — books, faces, puzzles, the world. A child who knows their eyes by name can also know their needs: it is too bright, I need to blink, my eyes are tired — the first steps of self-care for sight.

    What it teaches

    Body-part vocabulary, the seeing sense as a named ability, teamwork awareness (two eyes, one picture), self-protection habits, and observation games that train focus and visual attention.

    Words to learn

    eyesseeblinklookpairbright

    Say this to your child

    “"These are your eyes — one, two, a pair! They see the dog, the book, my face, everything. And they blink all by themselves, wash, blink, all day long, to keep themselves clean. Eyes are precious: gentle hands, no rubbing, and never looking at the sun. Deal?"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and count the eyes together: one, two — a pair. Ask what they do, then name it: they see.
    2. Find your child’s eyes in a mirror: point to each one, then blink together. The blink is automatic — point out that nobody decides to do it.
    3. Play the staring contest: who can keep both eyes open the longest without giggling? Then flip it — who can blink the fastest, five blinks in a row?
    4. Prove the teamwork: hold one finger in front of your child’s nose and watch both eyes swing to meet it. Two eyes, one job.
    5. Set the care rules gently: eyes get clean hands around them, no poking, and never a look at the sun. Eyes are precious, and precious things get care.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look at the picture together: how many eyes are in the picture? What color are they? What word sits above them? Are they open or closed?

    Ask your child

    "What do your eyes do?" "Why do we blink — who decided that?" "What did your eyes see first thing this morning?" "What do we never look at, even for a second?"

    What your child can say or do

    Your child may announce blink counts at breakfast, catch their own reflection and name both eyes, or warn a teddy solemnly about the sun — the seeing pair, named and defended.

    Out in the real world

    Eyes work everywhere: spotting the bus, finding the missing shoe, following a ladybug across a leaf, choosing the reddest apple. Name what the eyes found — "your eyes spotted it!" — and the pair gets credit for a full day of work.

    Try it together

    Eye-spy points: take turns being the caller — "something red!" "something round!" "something high up!" — and the finder must point with their eyes before their finger. It is visual search practice, colour review and turn-taking in one fast game.

    Understanding check

    Ask: "What do your eyes do? How many are there? Why do they blink?" The seeing, the pair and the self-washing answer — that is the lesson landed.

    Parent tips

    Do the finger-to-nose teamwork demo once with your own eyes too — feeling your own eyes swing is surprisingly delightful for adults. And treat the sun rule as absolute, not negotiable: eyes and sunshine meet through hats, shade and sunglasses only.

    Staying safe

    Eyes are delicate: dirty hands stay away from them, no poking or prodding, and looking straight at the sun — even briefly, even through clouds — can damage sight for life. Bright days get hats and shade; anything that lands in an eye gets a grown-up and clean water, fast.

    This lesson pairs with the Eyes flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Body Parts & Five Senses Flashcards.

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · BODY PARTS & FIVE SENSES FLASHCARDS · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Ears — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson tunes in to the hearing pair. Ears never sleep, never blink and never switch off — they catch the world all night and all day — and naming them opens up a whole set of listening games your house is already full of.

    What is this?

    Ears are the two hearing parts of the body, one on each side of the head. They catch sounds — voices, dogs, doorbells, songs, thunder — and pass them to the brain, which works out what each one is. Even asleep, ears stay on duty.

    What does it mean?

    Hearing is the one sense that never closes: eyes shut for sleep, but ears keep listening, which is why a familiar voice can wake a child and a lullaby can settle one. Sound arrives from every direction — front, back, through walls — making ears the body’s surround-sound system.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs to know: ears are for hearing, they come as a pair on the sides of the head, they work even when eyes are shut, and they are delicate — nothing ever goes inside an ear, and very loud noise right up close is too much for them.

    Why this matters

    Listening is half of every conversation and all of every song, story and instruction. A child who knows their ears can also train them: the quiet games in this lesson build the attention that circle time, music class and safety — hearing a warning call — all depend on.

    What it teaches

    Auditory attention and discrimination (telling sounds apart), body-part vocabulary, volume awareness, the quiet-stillness skill that group learning needs, and the sensory delight of a world heard with intent.

    Words to learn

    earshearlistensoundloudquiet

    Say this to your child

    “"These are your ears — one here, one here, a pair! They catch everything: my voice, the dog next door, the kettle, the song on the radio. They even listen while you sleep! And they are delicate — nothing ever goes inside an ear. Ears are for listening, from outside only."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and point: what are these, and what are they for? Name them — ears — and count: one on each side.
    2. Find your child’s ears: trace the curve, tug gently, then wiggle your own and admit how hard it is. Some people can, most cannot — trying is the fun.
    3. Play cover-and-listen: cup your hands over your ears and hear the world go quiet — then let go and name every sound that rushes back in.
    4. Prove the all-directions trick: your child shuts their eyes while you hide and call their name — the ears find you without any looking at all.
    5. Set the care rules: nothing goes in an ear, not even a finger, and ears need a break from very loud noise right up close. Ears are on duty for life.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look at the picture together: how many ears are in the picture? Where do they sit — on the sides? What word sits under them? Can you see a hole or a curve in each one?

    Ask your child

    "What do your ears do?" "What was the first sound you heard this morning?" "Do ears sleep when you sleep?" "What do we never put inside our ears?"

    What your child can say or do

    Your child may narrate the household soundscape — fridge humming, door creaking, daddy coughing — point out the ears of every animal they meet, or cup their hands behind their own ears and announce that the world got louder.

    Out in the real world

    Ears earn their keep everywhere: hearing the doorbell, the timer, the bath running, a sibling crying two rooms away, a warning shout at the road. Name the ears’ catches as they happen — "your ears heard that first!" — and the pair becomes a celebrated instrument.

    Try it together

    The sound detective: your child closes their eyes while you make a mystery sound — keys, a spoon in a cup, a page turning, a zipper — and they name it. Six sounds, six guesses, endless replays. It is listening, memory and deduction with objects from every drawer.

    Understanding check

    Ask: "What do your ears do? How many and where? What do we never put in them?" The hearing, the pair and the nothing-inside rule — that is the lesson landed.

    Parent tips

    The hide-and-call game doubles as separation reassurance — ears prove that a hidden parent is still findable. And keep music and screens at conversation volume as the household default: little ears do their best growing at that level, and the rule is easiest when it is everyone’s.

    Staying safe

    Nothing ever goes inside an ear — not fingers, not cotton buds, not toys; ears clean themselves, and anything stuck gets a doctor, not a dig. Loud sound close to the ear — shouts, speakers, headphones at full — can harm hearing, so keep volume at talking level and step back from the very loud.

    This lesson pairs with the Ears flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Body Parts & Five Senses Flashcards.

    Nose — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson puts the sniffer centre stage. The nose does three jobs at once — smelling, breathing, and being very good at finding bananas — and the sniffing games that teach it are the guaranteed-giggle kind your child will demand again tomorrow.

    What is this?

    The nose is the smelling part of the body, sitting in the middle of the face. It breathes air in and out through two little doorways, and it catches smells riding on that air — dinner cooking, flowers, rain, socks — and reports them all to the brain.

    What does it mean?

    Smell is the sneakiest sense: it works without being asked, and it is the fastest road to memory there is. One sniff of a familiar smell can bring back a whole place — grandma’s kitchen, the bakery, the swimming pool. The nose is a reporter sending invisible news upstairs.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs to know: the nose smells and breathes, sniffing is how it pulls smells up to be read, some smells are lovely and some are warnings — smoke, gone-off food — and nothing ever goes inside a nose, not fingers, not beans, not anything.

    Why this matters

    A named nose becomes a working nose. Children who can say what they smell join a whole layer of the world most people ignore — and smell is also a safety sense: burnt toast, smoke, spoiled milk all announce themselves to a nose that is listening.

    What it teaches

    Olfactory vocabulary and attention, breathing awareness (nose in, mouth out — the runner’s trick), the sniff-and-guess memory game, safety associations with warning smells, and the giggle engine of any good sniffing contest.

    Words to learn

    nosesmellsniffbreathestinkyfresh

    Say this to your child

    “"This is your nose — right in the middle, the best seat in the house! It breathes in and out all day and it smells everything: bananas, flowers, rain, dinner. Sniff, sniff — see? Sniffing pulls the smell up so your brain can read it. And nothing ever goes inside a nose. Noses sniff, that is all!"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and find the little nose: whose is it, and what is it for? Name it, then sniff the air dramatically to prove the point.
    2. Find your child’s nose in a mirror: touch it, wiggle it, breathe in and out through it and feel the air moving.
    3. Play the sniff test: three things with smells — a piece of fruit, a clean sock, a spoonful of something from the spice shelf — sniffed with eyes shut. Guess before you look.
    4. Teach the runner’s trick: breathe in through the nose, out through the mouth — in through the nose, out through the mouth. It is how noses and mouths share the work.
    5. Set the rule with a straight face: nothing goes in a nose. Not a finger, not a pea, not a bead. Noses are doorways, not cupboards.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look at the picture together: where does the little nose sit — in the middle of the face? What word is written beside it? Can you find your own nose without using your hands — by wiggling it?

    Ask your child

    "What does your nose do — all its jobs?" "What is the best smell in our house? The worst?" "How does sniffing help?" "What do we never put in our nose?"

    What your child can say or do

    Your child may sniff the air like a bloodhound at every meal, report dinner from the next room before it is announced, or patrol the house for stinky smells with the seriousness of an inspector — the nose, fully on duty.

    Out in the real world

    Noses work everywhere: the bread aisle at the shop, the rain on the walk home, the rubbish bin that needs taking out, the baby sibling’s head. Each smell is a sentence the nose writes — name a few, and the world gains a whole quiet channel.

    Try it together

    Sniff-and-guess kitchen: set out three covered cups, each hiding a smell — orange peel, a mint leaf, a dab of toothpaste. Sniff with eyes shut, guess, uncover, cheer. Rotate the cast daily; the nose gets sharper with practice, and the guessing never gets old.

    Understanding check

    Ask: "What does your nose do? What does sniffing do? What goes in a nose?" The two jobs, the pulling-up answer and the loud nothing — that is the lesson landed.

    Parent tips

    Keep the sniff test to food and kitchen smells — the safe category — and let your child add one mystery smell per round. If the guessing stalls, sniff together and compare notes out loud: two noses report differently, and comparing is the fun.

    Staying safe

    Nothing goes inside a nose — beads, beans, fingers and paper all end up in emergencies, and a nose is a doorway, not a drawer. Sniffing games use food and flowers only: cleaning products, spices up close and anything from a bottle under the sink stay off the list, and strong smells get sniffed from a distance.

    This lesson pairs with the Nose flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Body Parts & Five Senses Flashcards.

    Mouth — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson opens the busiest doorway on the face. The mouth takes in dinner, sends out words, shows the whole world a smile and hums along to every song — and your child has been running it, uncredited, since day one.

    What is this?

    The mouth is the opening below the nose, framed by lips. Food and drink go in, words and laughs and songs come out, and inside it works a team: teeth for chewing, tongue for tasting and moving, and a smile showing to everyone.

    What does it mean?

    The mouth is the body’s front door for two of its biggest jobs: fuel and language. Every word your child says travels out of this one doorway, shaped by lips and tongue; every bite that becomes energy travels in through it. It is also the sense-organ neighbour where taste happens — the tongue lives here.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs to know: the mouth eats, drinks, talks, smiles and hums, the lips frame it and the teeth and tongue work inside it, it opens wide for the dentist and says aaah — and only food and drink belong inside it, nothing else, not ever.

    Why this matters

    Naming the mouth gives your child a word for the place where eating meets talking meets feelings — the spot that hurts at the dentist, tingles at the toothbrush and aches when a wobbly tooth arrives. Body maps with the mouth on them handle all of those moments better.

    What it teaches

    Body-part vocabulary, oral-motor awareness (mouth shapes as controls), the food-and-words double duty, self-care links to tooth-brushing, and the safety rule that keeps non-food objects out.

    Words to learn

    mouthlipsteethtonguesmilechew

    Say this to your child

    “"This is your mouth — what a busy doorway! Food goes in, words come out, smiles show and songs hum. Inside: teeth chewing, tongue tasting, lips framing it all. Open wide — aaah! And remember the guest list: food and drink only. Everything else stays out of the mouth."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card: what body part is peeking out from behind this big open smile? Let the grin give it away, then name its jobs: it eats, it talks, it smiles.
    2. Make a mouth-shape show together: small ooh mouth, wide aah mouth, big smile, tiny hmm. Ask which shape the card is showing.
    3. Name the workmates: lips on the outside, teeth for chewing, tongue for tasting and moving food. Say aaah and find all three in a mirror.
    4. Talk through the door: put a hand gently on your lips while saying a word and feel the buzz. Every word your child says comes out of this doorway.
    5. Set the membership rule: mouths admit food, drink, words and toothbrushes — nothing else. Pebbles, crayons and toy parts stay out; the mouth has a guest list.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look at the picture together: is the mouth open or closed? Can you see a smile? What word sits beside it? Are any teeth showing?

    Ask your child

    "What are all the jobs your mouth does?" "What is inside your mouth that chews? That tastes?" "What shape is your mouth making right now?" "What belongs in a mouth — and what never does?"

    What your child can say or do

    Your child may perform the whole mouth-shape alphabet on request, report that the tongue lives inside and the teeth are its neighbours, or guard a pebble from a younger sibling with the guest-list rule quoted word for word.

    Out in the real world

    Mouths work everywhere: chewing dinner, blowing bubbles, whistling at the kettle, saying sorry, singing in the car. The dentist visit is the field trip — the wide-open aaah is exactly the mouth shape this lesson practised.

    Try it together

    Mouth-shape charades: you make a mouth shape — ooh, aah, wide smile, small circle — and your child guesses what goes with it: blowing a candle, saying aaah at the doctor, smiling at a friend, drinking through a straw. Swap roles. Every round is oral-motor practice disguised as a guessing game.

    Understanding check

    Ask: "Name three jobs your mouth does. What chews inside it? What goes in a mouth?" The list, the teeth and the food-only rule — that is the lesson landed.

    Parent tips

    Connect the mouth lesson to tooth-brushing night — same doorway, same teeth, same tongue — and the routine gains a body-map reason. If mouthing of objects still happens at three, the guest-list rule said cheerfully, and often, does more than any confiscation.

    Staying safe

    Only food and drink go in the mouth — pebbles, batteries, button coins and toy parts are mouth hazards, not snacks, and small objects stay away from little siblings. Biting is for food: friends, pets and furniture are all outside the guest list.

    This lesson pairs with the Mouth flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Body Parts & Five Senses Flashcards.

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · BODY PARTS & FIVE SENSES FLASHCARDS · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Hands — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson gives names to the busiest workers on the body. Hands grab, clap, wave, build, draw and help — they are how your child touches the whole world — and they come with their own care routine your child already half knows.

    What is this?

    Hands are the two grabbing parts at the ends of the arms, each with a palm and five fingers. They hold spoons and crayons, clap and wave, build towers, turn pages, stroke pets and help carry — nearly everything your child does with the world goes through the hands.

    What does it mean?

    Hands are the body’s main tool users — and its main touchers. Through the hands, your child learns what things feel like: smooth, bumpy, warm, soft. And hands are social too: they clap for friends, wave hello, point at wonders and reach out for comfort before any words get there.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs to know: hands hold, clap, wave and help, each hand has five fingers, they come as a left and a right, and they need care — washed before eating and after the toilet, dried, and kept gentle with friends and pets.

    Why this matters

    Hand skills are the school-readiness skills: holding crayons, turning pages, managing zips and buttons. Naming the hands and celebrating their work builds both vocabulary and pride — and the washing link turns a body-part lesson into a hygiene habit with a reason attached.

    What it teaches

    Fine-motor vocabulary and pride, hand preference as it emerges (left or right), touch learning through the palms, hygiene habits with meaning, and the social language of clapping, waving, pointing and helping.

    Words to learn

    handsfingersclapwaveholdwash

    Say this to your child

    “"These are your hands — two busy workers! They clap, they wave, they hold your spoon and build your towers. Five fingers each, a left and a right. And hands have rules: washed before we eat, gentle with our friends, and always helping. Show me your helping hands!"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card: two open hands in striped sleeves, fingers spread. Count the fingers on the card, then on your child’s real hand — five each.
    2. Name the jobs: clap, wave, hold, point, help. Do each one together — a clap, a wave, a spoon held up, a point at the window, a toy handed over.
    3. Play clap-fast-clap-slow: speed the claps up, slow them down, clap high, clap low, then hide both hands behind your back — where did they go?
    4. Introduce left and right: hold a hand up, thumb out — the L-shape is the left. Try both ways and see which one makes the letter.
    5. Finish with hand care: pretend to wash — palms, backs, between the fingers — and name the moments: before eating, after the toilet, after playing outside.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look at the picture together: how many hands are in the picture? Are the fingers open or closed? What do the sleeves look like — stripes? What word sits between the hands?

    Ask your child

    "What can your hands do — name five jobs!" "How many fingers does each hand have?" "Which hand is your left one?" "When do hands need washing?"

    What your child can say or do

    Your child may count all ten fingers twice a day, announce which hand is the drawing hand, or offer a helping hand at every chore with the phrase attached — the workers, named and proud.

    Out in the real world

    Hands are named all day: wash your hands, hold my hand at the road, clap for the birthday child, gentle hands with the cat. Each daily phrase is a repetition — and each one lands better on a child who knows exactly what a hand is.

    Try it together

    Helping-hands mission: give your child three real jobs that only hands can do — carry the spoons to the table, fold the tea towel, post the letter in the drawer. Narrate each as hand-work: your hands carried it, your hands folded it, your hands posted it. Pride follows the naming.

    Understanding check

    Ask: "What do hands do? How many fingers? When do we wash them?" The job list, the five and the before-eating answer — that is the lesson landed.

    Parent tips

    Follow your child’s lead on left versus right — preference settles by itself around this age, and forcing it slows it down. The L-trick is enough. And let helping hands be a real job title in the family: children work brilliantly for a title they hold.

    Staying safe

    Hands are for gentle: hitting, grabbing and throwing-at-friends are outside their job description, and the rule is easiest to teach as what hands are for, not just what they are not. Wash before eating and after the toilet — the palm-and-back-and-between-fingers way.

    This lesson pairs with the Hands flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Body Parts & Five Senses Flashcards.

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · BODY PARTS & FIVE SENSES FLASHCARDS · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Feet — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson gets down to the ground floor. Feet carry your child across every day of their life — and they are the bounciest body part to name, because foot games are standing games, and standing games are loud ones.

    What is this?

    Feet are the two walking parts at the bottom of the legs, each with a sole, a heel and five toes. They stand, walk, run, jump, kick, pedal and balance — every trip your child takes, the feet do the travelling.

    What does it mean?

    Feet are the body’s transport and its balance system: they tell the brain what the ground is like — soft rug, hard tiles, squishy grass — and adjust every step. That reporting is why barefoot play matters: feet learn the world best with nothing between them and it.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs to know: feet walk, run, jump and balance, ten toes live on them — five each — they report the ground to the brain, and they get care: socks when cold, shoes for outside, washed at bath time after a barefoot day.

    Why this matters

    Foot vocabulary powers the movement words preschool runs on — stand, jump, kick, tiptoe, stomp — and the games that teach it build real gross-motor control. A child who can go from giant stomp to mouse tiptoe on command has balance, listening and impulse control all in one game.

    What it teaches

    Gross-motor control (stomping, tiptoeing, freezing), balance and body awareness, foot vocabulary, counting to ten on toes, and self-care habits — socks, shoes, washing — with reasons attached.

    Words to learn

    feettoesstomptiptoejumpbalance

    Say this to your child

    “"These are your feet — the walkers, the jumpers, the runners! Ten toes on board, five on each. They can stomp like giants — STOMP STOMP — or sneak like mice on tiptoe, not a sound. And after all that walking, feet get washed, socks and shoes included. Feet are the bosses of going places."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card: two bare feet, toes included. Count the toes on the card, then on your child’s real feet — five per foot, ten altogether.
    2. Name the jobs: stand, walk, run, jump, kick, tiptoe. Try each one on the spot — a jump, a kick in the air, a wobbly balance on one foot.
    3. Play stomp-and-tiptoe: stomp like a giant — loud, heavy, shaking the floor — then switch to tiptoe like a mouse, small and silent. Alternate on your call.
    4. Add the freeze: after any stomp or tiptoe round, call freeze! — both feet still, balancing. Freezing is the hard part and the funny one.
    5. Finish with feet care: socks when the floor is cold, shoes for outside, washed at bath time. Feet work all day; they get looked after at night.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look at the picture together: are these bare feet or do they have shoes on? How many toes can you count? What word sits above them? Are the feet side by side or one in front?

    Ask your child

    "What do your feet do all day?" "How many toes — on each foot, and altogether?" "Show me a giant stomp. Now a mouse tiptoe." "What do feet wear outside?"

    What your child can say or do

    Your child may stomp-tiptoe-freeze through the hallway on request, count all ten toes at bath time, or demand barefoot time as a grass-reporting mission — the transport department, fully staffed and proud.

    Out in the real world

    Feet mark every journey: the walk to the park, the pedal on the trike, the kick of the ball, the wobble across a stepping stone. Name the work — your feet climbed it, your feet pedalled it — and the bottom of the body gets the credit it earns.

    Try it together

    Stomp-and-freeze parade: music on, everyone marches; the music stops, you call a foot command — freeze, tiptoe, jump, stand on one foot — and everyone obeys until the next round. The switching is the training: big moves, small moves, stillness, all on one word.

    Understanding check

    Ask: "What do feet do? How many toes? Show me tiptoe — now freeze." The list, the ten and a wobbly balanced freeze — that is the lesson landed.

    Parent tips

    Give barefoot minutes on safe floors and real grass: the ground-reporting is the point, and children love naming what their soles found. And keep the stomp games off tiles with sleeping babies — feet lessons are best held on rugs and lawns.

    Staying safe

    Feet meet the world first: watch for hot pavement in summer, sharp things on lawns and slippery socks on wooden stairs — grip socks or bare feet for climbing, shoes for outside, and a grown-up for anything that stings.

    This lesson pairs with the Feet flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Body Parts & Five Senses Flashcards.

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · BODY PARTS & FIVE SENSES FLASHCARDS · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Arms — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson reaches out. Arms are the long levers between shoulders and hands — they lift, swing, wrap and carry — and they are the body part your child uses most for the things that matter most: holding on and hugging.

    What is this?

    Arms are the two long parts between the shoulders and the hands. They reach up high, stretch out wide, lift and carry, swing when walking, and wrap around for hugs. At the end of every arm is a hand — the arms deliver it wherever it needs to go.

    What does it mean?

    Arms are the delivery system for the hands: everything hands do, arms reach for first. They are also the hug machines — the wrap-around part of every cuddle — and the balancers, flung out wide whenever a beam or a curb needs crossing.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs to know: arms reach, lift, carry, swing and hug, they connect the shoulders to the hands, they stretch in three useful shapes — up like a tree, out like an airplane, around like a hug — and sleeves are the tunnels arms travel through when dressing.

    Why this matters

    Arm strength and control power the whole preschool day: climbing, carrying chairs, painting big, catching balls. Naming the arms and playing their shapes builds the vocabulary of movement — reach, lift, stretch, wrap — that PE lessons and playgrounds run on.

    What it teaches

    Gross-motor reach, lift and carry strength, spatial language (up, out, around), dressing independence through sleeve practice, and the emotional work of hugging — arms as the instruments of comfort.

    Words to learn

    armshugreachliftstretchswing

    Say this to your child

    “"These are your arms — the long reachers! They lift, they carry, they swing when you walk, and they wrap around for the very best hugs. Up like a tree… out like an airplane… around like a hug! And every sleeve is a tunnel your arm travels through. Ready for cargo?"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card: two arms reaching down from purple sleeves, hands open. Ask what they are doing, then name them: arms.
    2. Find your child’s arms: trace from shoulder to hand. Squeeze gently — the arm is the long part that delivers the hand.
    3. Play the three shapes: arms up like a tree, arms out like an airplane, arms wrapped around your own body like a self-hug. Hold each one for three seconds.
    4. Test the lifting: hand your child a light bag, a cushion, a teddy — the arms carry it across the room. Real cargo makes real pride.
    5. Finish with the sleeve game: push one hand through a sleeve and out the other end — where did it go? Arm in, arm out, arm through: dressing is arms practice.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look at the picture together: what are the arms doing — reaching down? Are the hands open? What color are the sleeves? What word sits with the arms?

    Ask your child

    "What do your arms do?" "Show me all three arm shapes — tree, airplane, hug." "What did your arms carry today?" "What is the tunnel arms go through when we dress?"

    What your child can say or do

    Your child may deliver the three arm shapes as a daily routine, report every carried object as arm-work, or wrap both arms around your neck at pickup with the word attached — hug delivered, by name.

    Out in the real world

    Arms work everywhere: reaching the top shelf of the cupboard, carrying the shopping bag one seat over, swinging on the monkey bars, wrapping around a friend who fell down. Name the reach, the carry, the wrap — the levers get their credit.

    Try it together

    Arm-o-rama circuit: five stations around the room — reach up high and touch the doorframe, out wide and spin like an airplane, around for a self-hug, lift the cushion and carry it one lap, swing both arms like a windmill. Ten seconds each, then swap leadership. Every station is a different arm verb.

    Understanding check

    Ask: "What do arms do? Show me the three shapes. What connects your shoulder to your hand?" The verbs, the shapes and the arm answer — that is the lesson landed.

    Parent tips

    Let the hug be part of the lesson, not just a shape — arms learn their job by doing it. And use the sleeve tunnel at dressing time every morning: naming the arm going through turns a daily battle into a body-part game with a winner.

    Staying safe

    Arms are for reaching, lifting and hugging — never for swinging at people or yanking toys; the rule sticks best when the good jobs are praised loudly. Lift with two arms for heavy things, and hands get help from a grown-up for anything hot or sharp.

    This lesson pairs with the Arms flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Body Parts & Five Senses Flashcards.

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · BODY PARTS & FIVE SENSES FLASHCARDS · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Legs — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson marches in the biggest movers of all. Legs do the going — walking, running, hopping, kicking, climbing — and the games that name them are the kind your child will want to keep playing long after the lesson ends.

    What is this?

    Legs are the two long parts between the hips and the feet. They stand, walk, run, jump, hop, kick and climb — every place your child gets to, the legs get them there. At the bottom of each leg is a foot, the part that meets the ground.

    What does it mean?

    Legs are the body’s engines, and feet are their wheels: the legs make the power, the feet steer and land it. Together they carry the whole body through the day — and they are also the strongest muscles your child owns, which is why running feels so good.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs to know: legs walk, run, jump, hop and kick, each leg ends in a foot, one-leg standing is the legs’ balance trick and it takes practice, and legs get care too — trousers on, shoes tied, rest when they are tired.

    Why this matters

    Leg vocabulary and leg strength grow together. The marching, hopping and one-leg games build the coordination that playgrounds demand, and naming the legs means a child can say what hurts, what is tired and what just did something brilliant.

    What it teaches

    Gross-motor power and coordination, single-leg balance (a genuine milestone skill), movement vocabulary, body-part naming below the waist — often the last to be learned — and the stamina pride of a body that goes and goes.

    Words to learn

    legswalkrunhopkickclimb

    Say this to your child

    “"These are your legs — the strongest engines you own! They walk, they run, they jump, they kick, they climb. In the middle is your knee, the hinge that folds. Can you march like a soldier? Hop like a bunny? Stand on one leg like a flamingo? Your legs just did the whole circus!"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card: two legs in purple shorts, standing ready. Ask what they are for, then name them: legs — the body’s engines.
    2. Find your child’s legs: trace from hip to foot. Bend a knee together and feel how the leg folds — the knee is the hinge in the middle.
    3. Play the engine games: march around the room with high knees, then run on the spot, then a big two-foot jump. The legs are warming up.
    4. Hold the balance challenge: stand on one leg like a flamingo — count how long, try the other leg, then hold a teddy for difficulty. Flamingos are allowed to wobble.
    5. Finish with the carrying idea: everything your child reaches — the park, the slide, the top of the stairs — the legs carried them there. Thank the engines out loud.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look at the picture together: how many legs are in the picture? What are they wearing — purple shorts? What word sits with the legs? Are they standing still or moving?

    Ask your child

    "What do your legs do all day?" "Where is your knee — show me the hinge!" "Can you hop on one leg — how many hops?" "What did your legs carry you to today?"

    What your child can say or do

    Your child may march through every doorway for a week, demand flamingo-timing contests with the whole family, or report that legs are the strongest muscles and offer to prove it — engines named, pride installed.

    Out in the real world

    Legs are named all day: legs up for the trousers, run to the gate, kick the ball, climb the slide, walk to the bus. The playground is the field trip — every apparatus there is a legs lesson already running.

    Try it together

    Legs circuit: four stations — march ten steps, five two-foot jumps, three hops on each leg, one long balance on one foot with arms out like wings. Run the circuit twice, then let your child design a station for you. Designing is the highest level of knowing.

    Understanding check

    Ask: "What do legs do? Where is the knee? Show me one-leg balance." The verbs, the hinge and a wobbly flamingo — that is the lesson landed.

    Parent tips

    Count hops and balance-seconds out loud — the numbers give the game a target and sneak in counting. And expect the flamingo to beat some adults in the family; letting your child win the balance contest is a small price for a body part this loved.

    Staying safe

    Legs run fast — indoor running lives on rugs, not tiles, and climbing happens with a grown-up in sight. Knees take the falls: patches and plasters are part of the engine’s maintenance, and tired legs are allowed to say so.

    This lesson pairs with the Legs flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Body Parts & Five Senses Flashcards.

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · BODY PARTS & FIVE SENSES FLASHCARDS · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    See — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson opens the five-senses collection with the busiest one. Seeing is how your child takes in most of the world — and this card proves it beautifully: a butterfly has landed right where the eyes can find it.

    What is this?

    See is what your eyes do: catch light and turn it into pictures inside your head. It is one of the body’s five senses — the five ways to learn about the world — and it is the one working hardest for your child, from the moment the day starts.

    What does it mean?

    Your body has five ways to learn: eyes see, ears hear, nose smells, tongue tastes, skin touches. Seeing is the loudest of the five — most of what a preschooler knows arrived through the eyes. And seeing is a skill, not just a fact: looking closely, like the picture’s butterfly-watcher, is seeing done on purpose.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs to know: we see with our eyes, seeing is one of five senses, looking closely is something you can practise — slow down, really look — and eyes need protection: never a look at the sun, bright days get hats and shade.

    Why this matters

    Naming see gives your child the owner’s manual for their busiest sense. It turns look at this into a game they can play alone — spotting, noticing, comparing — and it anchors the five-senses map that every later science lesson, from light to rainbows, will stand on.

    What it teaches

    Visual attention and observation, the five-senses framework (seeing as one of five), descriptive vocabulary for what the eyes find, sun-safety habits, and the quiet pride of spotting things others miss.

    Words to learn

    seeeyeslookspotbutterflyobserve

    Say this to your child

    “"See! Your eyes are one of your five senses — five ways your body learns about the world. The butterfly on this card landed right where the eyes could find it. Let us play: I see something red… can you spot it? Looking closely is seeing done like a scientist."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and ask what the eyes are doing — and what has come to visit them. A butterfly, landing near! That is seeing at work: the eyes found it.
    2. Name the five-senses family: eyes see, ears hear, nose smells, tongue tastes, skin touches. Seeing is the first of five ways to learn.
    3. Play colour spy: I see something red… something round… something tiny. The finder must point before shouting the answer — looking before leaping.
    4. Practise looking closely: pick one small thing — a leaf, a button, a toy — and study it for ten slow seconds. What did the eyes catch that a quick look missed?
    5. Set the sun rule with care: the sun is too bright for eyes, ever. Bright days get hats, shade and sunglasses — the eyes do the seeing, the hat does the guarding.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look at the picture together: what has landed near the eyes — a butterfly? Is it close or far away? What word sits with the picture? What color can you spot in it?

    Ask your child

    "What do we see with?" "How many senses does your body have — can you name them?" "What did your eyes spot today that nobody else noticed?" "Why do we never look at the sun?"

    What your child can say or do

    Your child may announce the five senses as a memorised team, spot the tiniest ladybug on the walk and demand witnesses, or hold up the sun rule to a grandparent — seeing, named, practised and defended.

    Out in the real world

    Seeing is the sense that works everywhere: reading signs, spotting the bus, choosing the best apple, finding a friend in the park. Give the eyes their credit out loud — your eyes found it — and the sense becomes a skill your child knows they own.

    Try it together

    Spot-the-change: arrange five toys on a tray, let your child look away, secretly remove or swap one, and ask what changed. Three rounds, then swap roles. It is observation training with a mystery plot — and remembering what was there is the hard, valuable part.

    Understanding check

    Ask: "What do we see with? How many senses are there? Show me looking closely." The eyes, the five and a slow deliberate stare — that is the lesson landed.

    Parent tips

    Keep the colour spy game in the car, the queue and the bath — it is the most portable sense game there is. And when your child spots something first, let them be the spy-caller next round: the finder becomes the teacher, and the sense gets sharpened twice.

    Staying safe

    The sun rule is absolute: looking straight at the sun — even for a second, even on a hazy day — can damage eyes for life. Hats, shade and sunglasses are the eye’s equipment for bright days, and adults follow the same rule out loud so the copying goes both ways.

    This lesson pairs with the See flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Body Parts & Five Senses Flashcards.

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · BODY PARTS & FIVE SENSES FLASHCARDS · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Hear — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson tunes the five-senses collection to sound. Hearing is the sense that never closes — working in the dark, through walls, while asleep — and this card draws it beautifully: sound waves rippling out of the picture, straight for an ear.

    What is this?

    Hear is what your ears do: catch sounds — voices, dogs, rain, music — and send them to the brain to be understood. It is the second of the five senses, and the only one that never switches off for sleep.

    What does it mean?

    Sound travels in invisible waves through the air — the card draws them as ripples — and the ear collects them. Hearing works from every direction at once, even through doors and in the dark, which makes it the body’s early-warning system: the sense that tells you something is happening before you can see what.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs to know: we hear with our ears, hearing is the second of the five senses, sounds can be loud or soft, near or far, and ears are delicate — very loud noise right up close hurts them, so volume stays kind and ears get quiet when they need it.

    Why this matters

    Hearing is half of language: every word your child learns arrives through this sense first. The listening games build the attention that stories, music and classroom instructions run on — and a trained ear is also a safety ear, catching the warning shout before the eye finds the danger.

    What it teaches

    Auditory attention and discrimination, the five-senses framework (hearing as one of five), volume awareness and self-regulation, sound vocabulary (loud, soft, high, low, near, far), and stillness as the price of listening well.

    Words to learn

    hearearssoundloudsoftwaves

    Say this to your child

    “"Hear! Your ears catch sounds in invisible waves — listen: the clock, the bird, my voice. Hearing is one of your five senses, and it never sleeps — your ears work even in the dark! But they are delicate, so sounds stay kind and gentle around them. What can you hear right now, this very second?"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and ask what the ripples around the ear might be. Explain: sound travels in waves — invisible, but real — and the ear catches them. That is hearing.
    2. Name the five-senses family again: seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching. Hearing is number two — and it works even with eyes shut.
    3. Prove it: everyone shuts their eyes for five slow seconds and listens. What arrived? Name every sound that came in — the fridge, a car, a voice down the hall.
    4. Play near-and-far: make a sound close to your child’s ear, then the same sound from across the room. Same sound, different size — that is how ears measure distance.
    5. Set the volume rule: ears like sounds at talking level. Shouting straight into an ear, or music at full blast, is too much — quiet is not boring, quiet is ear care.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look at the picture together: what do you see coming from the ear — the purple waves? What word sits with the picture? Is the ear alone or with a face?

    Ask your child

    "What do we hear with?" "Which sense keeps working while you sleep?" "What sounds can you hear right now?" "What sounds are too loud for ears — and what do we do about it?"

    What your child can say or do

    Your child may freeze mid-play, finger raised, to announce a sound nobody else noticed, ask what made every noise in the house, or turn the music down unprompted with the volume rule quoted — hearing, owned and defended.

    Out in the real world

    Hearing fills every part of the day: the kettle, the doorbell, the story at bedtime, the warning call at the road. Give the ears their catches — your ears heard the post arrive — and the invisible sense becomes visible to its owner.

    Try it together

    The listening minute: sit still together, eyes open or shut, and raise one finger for every new sound heard in one quiet minute. Compare lists afterwards — two ears, two different reports. The stillness is the training; the comparison is the fun.

    Understanding check

    Ask: "What do we hear with? How many senses? What do sound waves look like on our card?" The ears, the five and the ripples — that is the lesson landed.

    Parent tips

    The listening minute works in waiting rooms, queues and cars — anywhere stillness is welcome anyway. And model your own listening: when a sound arrives, stop, name it, look for it together. Children learn what attention looks like by watching yours.

    Staying safe

    Little ears are delicate: keep music and screens at talking volume, no shouting directly into anyone’s ear, and step away from very loud noise — speakers, engines, fireworks — or cover ears when it cannot be avoided. Ringing ears are ears asking for quiet.

    This lesson pairs with the Hear flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Body Parts & Five Senses Flashcards.

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · BODY PARTS & FIVE SENSES FLASHCARDS · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Smell — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson follows the nose into the five-senses collection. Smelling is the sneakiest sense — working all day without being asked — and this card gives it a worthy subject: a purple flower, sniffed up close, in full bloom.

    What is this?

    Smell is what your nose does: catch scents riding on the air and report them to the brain. It is the third of the five senses — the nose’s very own way of learning about the world — and the fastest one: a single sniff can announce dinner, rain or a flower before any word is spoken.

    What does it mean?

    Smells travel invisibly, like the sound waves did — tiny pieces of the world drifting through the air — and the nose pulls them up with a sniff. Smell is also the memory sense: a single whiff of a known smell can fetch a whole place back, which is why noses keep grandma’s kitchen better than cameras do.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs to know: we smell with our noses, smelling is the third of the five senses, sniffing pulls smells up to be read, some smells are treats and some are warnings — smoke, spoiled food — and sniffing games use food and flowers only.

    Why this matters

    A named nose becomes a working nose, and smell is a safety sense as much as a pleasure one: burnt toast, gas, gone-off milk all announce themselves to whoever is listening. The sniff-and-guess game also builds vocabulary fast — every smell wants its word.

    What it teaches

    Olfactory attention and vocabulary, the five-senses framework (smelling as one of five), memory-through-scent connections, warning-smell associations, and the gentle sniff technique — small sips of air, not great gulps.

    Words to learn

    smellnosesniffscentfreshstinky

    Say this to your child

    “"Smell! Your nose catches scents in the air — sniff, sniff, gently, like a small sip. Smelling is one of your five senses, and it is the fastest: one sniff and you know dinner is ready. Some smells are treats — flowers, bananas, clean washing. Some are warnings — smoke means find a grown-up, fast. What does the air smell like right now?"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and ask what the nose is doing — sniffing a flower! That is the sense called smell, number three of five.
    2. Demonstrate the gentle sniff: a small sip of air through the nose, not a great gulp. Practise on the air in the room — what does here smell like?
    3. Play sniff-and-guess: three covered cups hiding smells — orange peel, a mint leaf, a dab of jam. Eyes shut, sniff, guess, uncover, cheer.
    4. Sort the smells: which were treats and which would be warnings? Name the warning crew — smoke, rotten food, something burnt — smells that mean find a grown-up.
    5. Take the game outside or to the garden: flowers, wet grass after rain, the herb shelf. The world is a smell library, and the nose has a card.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look at the picture together: what is the nose sniffing — a purple flower? Is the flower close to the nose or far away? What word sits beside them? What color is the flower?

    Ask your child

    "What do we smell with?" "Which sense is the fastest — the one that knows dinner before anyone says so?" "What is the best smell in our house?" "What smells mean find a grown-up?"

    What your child can say or do

    Your child may smell every meal from the doorway and announce the menu, report the rain before it arrives, or patrol the flowers with slow deliberate sniffs — the nose, promoted from breathing equipment to chief investigator.

    Out in the real world

    Smell reports arrive all day: bread in the bakery aisle, the swimming pool, the rubbish bin, the baby’s head, rain on hot pavement. Name two or three a day — what does your nose say? — and a quiet sense becomes a loud part of the family vocabulary.

    Try it together

    The smell library: collect three or four safe smells in little cups — lemon peel, cinnamon, a pine needle, a coffee bean — sniff with eyes shut and guess. Swap in new smells weekly. Memory and vocabulary grow with every round, and the guessing stays funny forever.

    Understanding check

    Ask: "What do we smell with? How do we sniff — big gulp or small sip? What smells mean find a grown-up?" The nose, the sip and the warning list — that is the lesson landed.

    Parent tips

    Keep the smell library to food, herbs and flowers — the safe shelf — and let your child nominate one new smell a week: ownership keeps the game alive. And honour every wrong guess with a sniff-along: comparing notes is where the vocabulary actually gets built.

    Staying safe

    Sniffing games use food, herbs and flowers only — cleaning sprays, spices held close and anything from under the sink stay off the list, and unknown bottles are find-a-grown-up objects, never sniffed. Gentle sips of air, never deep gulps of anything strong.

    This lesson pairs with the Smell flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Body Parts & Five Senses Flashcards.

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · BODY PARTS & FIVE SENSES FLASHCARDS · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Fingers — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson counts what your child already carries everywhere. Fingers are the counting set that came free at birth — five per hand, ten in total — and the finest tools the body owns, already at work on buttons, crayons and page corners.

    What is this?

    Fingers are the five long parts at the end of each hand — a thumb and four fingers. They wiggle, point, grab, pinch and count, and they do the fine work: buttons, zips, page turns, puzzle pieces, pencil grips. Every hand comes with the full set, five per hand.

    What does it mean?

    Fingers are the body’s precision team: the arms reach, the hands hold, and the fingers do the detail. Each one has a speciality — the thumb can touch every other finger, which is why holding anything works; the pointing finger leads the eye; the smallest one sneaks into the tiniest spaces.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs to know: each hand has five fingers, ten on both hands together, they can be counted — which makes them the friendliest maths lesson there is — and each has a job: thumb for grabbing, one for pointing, all of them for wiggling on request.

    Why this matters

    Finger naming is counting’s natural on-ramp: most children count their fingers before they count anything else, and the counting sticks because the objects are always attached. Fine-finger control is also the school-readiness skill underneath every crayon, zip and scissors job to come.

    What it teaches

    Counting and one-to-one correspondence, fine-motor isolation (moving one finger at a time is genuinely hard), hand preference, pointing as communication, and the finger-play tradition — rhymes and games that train every finger in order.

    Words to learn

    fingersthumbfivecountwigglepoint

    Say this to your child

    “"These are your fingers — five on every hand, ten altogether! They wiggle, they point, they grab, they count. The thumb can touch every single fingertip — try it! And they are the counting set you were born with: one, two, three, four, five. Show me one finger wiggling all by itself!"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and count the fingers on the open hand: one, two, three, four, five. Then count your child’s real hand to check the set is complete.
    2. Wiggle test: can your child wiggle just one finger, then two, then all five like a piano? Moving one finger alone is a real skill — celebrate every success.
    3. Name the special jobs: the thumb that touches every fingertip, the pointer that shows the way, the little one that fits the small spaces. Try each job out.
    4. Play hide-and-seek fingers: hide all five in a fist, then let one peek out — can your child name which one? Thumb? Pointer? Guessing is half the game.
    5. Give the fingers real work: a button, a zipper, a page to turn, a puzzle piece to place. Fingers learn by doing — and the doing is the lesson.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look at the picture together: how many fingers does the open hand show? Is the thumb among them? What word sits with the hand? Are the fingers spread out or curled?

    Ask your child

    "How many fingers on one hand? On both hands?" "Can you wiggle just your thumb — now just your pointing finger?" "What is your pointing finger for?" "What did your fingers learn to do this week?"

    What your child can say or do

    Your child may count to ten on fingers at every opportunity, show off a one-finger wiggle like a party trick, or use the pointing finger to lead the whole family to what matters — the counting set, fully operational.

    Out in the real world

    Fingers work everywhere: turning book pages, fastening shoes, picking berries, counting out apple slices, pressing doorbells. Name the finger-work as it happens — your fingers buttoned it, your fingers counted it — and the fine team gets its reviews.

    Try it together

    Finger football: fingers lined up as teams on the table edge, one ball (a soft pom-pom), and flicking only — which finger can shoot the pom-pom across the table? Each finger gets a turn. Precision flicking is finger isolation training in World Cup packaging.

    Understanding check

    Ask: "How many fingers on each hand? Which one touches all the others? Show me a single-finger wiggle." The count, the thumb and the wiggle — that is the lesson landed.

    Parent tips

    Fingerplays — rhymes with finger actions — are the tradition for good reason: they train isolation, counting and rhythm in one sitting. Learn two or three by heart and keep them for queues and car seats. And never rush pencil grip: fingers that wiggle freely now will hold pencils properly later.

    Staying safe

    Fingers and doors do not mix — keep them clear of hinges and edges, and fingers and small objects need the choking rule around babies. Fingernails get trimmed by a grown-up; the picking and poking jobs belong to the fingers, not the fingernails.

    This lesson pairs with the Fingers flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Body Parts & Five Senses Flashcards.

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · BODY PARTS & FIVE SENSES FLASHCARDS · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Toes — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson goes to the very end of the body, where the counting and the tickling live. Toes are the fingers’ ground crew — five per foot, ten in total — and the games that name them come with the best sound effects in the whole set.

    What is this?

    Toes are the five small parts at the end of each foot — ten altogether. They wiggle, grip, push and balance: every step your child takes, the toes press the ground and hold on. The big toe is the boss one; the littlest ones ride along.

    What does it mean?

    Toes are the body’s grip team and its balancing crew. Press your toes down and you can stand taller; spread them and you can balance wider. They are also the most ticklish address on the body, which is why toe games come with laughter built in — and why counting them sticks better than counting anything else.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs to know: each foot has five toes, ten on both feet, the big toe is the leader, toes help balance and grip — try picking up a sock with your toes — and they get care too: socks when cold, shoes that fit, toenails trimmed by a grown-up.

    Why this matters

    Toe counting is the second verse of finger counting, and it locks in numbers to ten. Knowing the toes also gives your child words for the shoe shop, the bath and the doctor — and the toe-wiggle games build the foot strength that barefoot running and balance need.

    What it teaches

    Counting to ten across two feet, toe isolation and strength (wiggling one toe is the hard mode), balance and grip awareness, body-part naming at the extremities, and the tickle-and-giggle bonding that keeps the lesson requested.

    Words to learn

    toestenwiggleticklegripbalance

    Say this to your child

    “"These are your toes — ten little ones, five on each foot! They wiggle, they grip, they balance you. The big toe is the boss — try to wiggle just the bosses! And they are the tickliest spot on your whole body, which is why we count them like this: one, two, three, four, five… and here comes the tickle!"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and count the toes: one to five on the card, then one to five on your child’s real foot, then both feet — all the way to ten.
    2. Wiggle test: can all ten wiggle at once? Can just the big toes — the boss toes — wiggle on their own? Try it together; it is harder than it sounds.
    3. Test the grip: lay a sock or a small cloth on the floor and pick it up with toes only. Ten toes, one sock, no hands — the room will roar.
    4. Try the balance trick: stand tall and press the toes into the floor — feel how the toes hold you up. Then lift the toes and feel the wobble arrive.
    5. Finish with toe care: socks when cold, shoes that fit, toenails cut by a grown-up. Toes work inside shoes all day; they get air-time at bath time.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look at the picture together: how many toes can you count on the feet? Are they big, little, or both? What word sits above them? Are the toes lined up in a row?

    Ask your child

    "How many toes on each foot — and altogether?" "Which toe is the boss?" "Can you pick up a sock with your toes?" "Who is the tickliest person in this family?"

    What your child can say or do

    Your child may demand the toe-counting-with-tickle finish at every nappy change of a sibling, walk around gripping a sock in each foot, or announce the boss toes at the shoe shop — ten counted, grip tested, laughter banked.

    Out in the real world

    Toes appear at bath time, the shoe shop, the beach and the paddling pool — sand between toes is a whole report. Name the grip at work: your toes held the ladder, your toes balanced the beam — the ground crew gets the review.

    Try it together

    Toe tug-of-war: sit facing your child, feet touching, and hook toes together gently — pull! Whoever unhooks loses. It is toe strength, giggle fuel and a fair fight the small ones often win. Follow with the sock pickup championship for the quiet version.

    Understanding check

    Ask: "How many toes altogether? Which one is the boss? Show me a toe grip." The ten, the big toe and the sock pickup — that is the lesson landed.

    Parent tips

    Keep the tickle at the end of the count — the numbers buy the tickle, which keeps the counting requested. And give toes barefoot minutes on safe surfaces: grip and balance grow strongest when the ground crew meets the ground directly.

    Staying safe

    Toenails get trimmed by a grown-up, straight across, and shoes that fit beat shoes that will-fit-eventually — squeezed toes complain for years. Barefoot play happens on checked floors and clean grass; the toilet-paper-tube rule applies to anything toe-sized near babies.

    This lesson pairs with the Toes flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Body Parts & Five Senses Flashcards.

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · BODY PARTS & FIVE SENSES FLASHCARDS · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Skin — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson meets the sense that goes everywhere the body goes. Skin covers the whole body — arms, cheeks, the tip of the nose — and it is doing two jobs at once: keeping the body safely in, and reporting what the world feels like.

    What is this?

    Skin is the covering that wraps the whole body — and it is the touch sense itself. It reports warm and cool, soft and hard, bumpy and smooth, dry and wet, and it sends the warnings too: too hot, too sharp, something crawling.

    What does it mean?

    Skin is the body’s largest sense organ, and the only one worn everywhere. Touch is the fifth of the five senses — eyes see, ears hear, nose smells, tongue tastes, and skin does the feeling. It is also the body’s coat: it keeps the inside in, the weather out, and heals itself when it gets a scrape.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs to know: skin covers the whole body and it is how we feel things, touch is the fifth sense, skin reports the world — warm water, cool tiles, a soft cat, a scratchy jumper — and it needs care: washes, plasters for scrapes, and sun hats on bright days.

    Why this matters

    Touch is the first sense a baby ever used — held, wrapped, rocked — and it stays the comfort sense for life: a hug is skin talking. Naming skin gives your child words for comfort and for warning — this jumper scratches, that radiator burns — and both kinds of sentence matter.

    What it teaches

    Tactile vocabulary (warm, cool, soft, rough, smooth, bumpy), the five-senses framework (touch as the fifth), body coverage awareness — skin is everywhere — and the self-care links: washing, plasters, sun protection.

    Words to learn

    skintouchwarmcoolsoftscratchy

    Say this to your child

    “"This is skin — it covers you everywhere! Your arms, your cheeks, the tip of your nose: all skin. It is your touch sense, the fifth of your five senses — it feels warm and cool, soft and scratchy, and it tells your brain everything. Skin is also your coat: it keeps you in and the world out. Take care of your coat!"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and ask what the close-up picture might be. Reveal it: skin — the covering on your whole body, and the feeling sense itself.
    2. Prove the coverage: skin on the arm, skin on the cheek, skin on the nose, skin on the tummy. It is everywhere you look — the body’s own coat.
    3. Play the two-bowl test: one bowl of warm water, one of cool. One hand in each, then report — warm, cool! The skin told you which was which, instantly.
    4. Read textures: a soft blanket, a bumpy towel, a smooth table, a scratchy jumper. Touch each and say the word the skin sent.
    5. Finish with skin care: washes keep it clean, plasters look after scrapes, sun hats guard it on bright days. The coat does a lot — it earns its maintenance.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look at the picture together: what does the close-up show — a patch of skin? What word sits with it? Is the skin smooth or bumpy in the picture? Where does your own skin show right now?

    Ask your child

    "What covers your whole body?" "Which sense is skin — number five of how many?" "What did your skin feel today — warm? cool? soft?" "How do we take care of skin?"

    What your child can say or do

    Your child may report textures all day — the rug is fluffy, the window is cold — ask for a plaster with dignity when a scrape arrives, or announce that the bath water is warm and the tiles are cool, both confirmed by the fifth sense.

    Out in the real world

    Skin reports arrive constantly: bath water tested with a toe, the cat’s fur, granny’s scratchy scarf, the sun-warmed slide. Name the reports as they come — your skin told you that — and the touch sense becomes a working vocabulary instead of a feeling without words.

    Try it together

    The texture trail: line up four safe textures along the floor — blanket, bubble wrap, towel, smooth cushion — and walk them barefoot, naming each underfoot feeling. Then do it with eyes shut. The feet have skin too, and the trail proves it.

    Understanding check

    Ask: "What covers your body? Which sense is it? What did your skin feel today?" The covering, the fifth and a texture or two — that is the lesson landed.

    Parent tips

    Keep a texture basket — fabric squares, a sponge, a pinecone, a smooth stone — and rotate it weekly; the skin learns like the ears do, by comparison. And treat every plaster ceremony as skin science: the coat got a rip, the plaster is the repair, the body heals it itself.

    Staying safe

    Skin reports pain for a reason — hot things, sharp things and broken glass are look-don’t-touch, and the warning gets obeyed, not tested. Scrapes get washed and covered; burns get cold water and a grown-up, fast. Sun hats and sunscreen are the coat’s weather gear.
