    This lesson pairs with the Skin flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Body Parts & Five Senses Flashcards.

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · BODY PARTS & FIVE SENSES FLASHCARDS · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Tongue — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson meets the body’s show-off. The tongue hides all day behind the teeth and then, on request, peeks out — and between the silliness it does two serious jobs: tasting every bite and shaping every word.

    What is this?

    The tongue is the pink muscle that lives inside the mouth. It tastes the food, moves the food where chewing needs it, and shapes the sounds that become words. It can go up, out, side to side and curl — the busiest muscle your child owns.

    What does it mean?

    The tongue is a muscle that never stops: it stirs every bite, checks every temperature, presses every sound into shape — the same tongue says llama and lollipop — and then cleans the teeth afterwards. It is also where the taste sense lives: sweet, salty, sour and more, all reported from this one pink floor of the mouth.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs to know: the tongue lives inside the mouth, it tastes the food — one of the five senses happens right here — it helps make every word, it can peek out and go back in on request, and it stays inside for eating and talking: peeking is a game, not a habit.

    Why this matters

    The tongue is where eating meets speaking — the two hardest jobs a preschooler’s body does. Playing with it builds the oral-motor control that clear speech runs on, and naming it gives your child the word for the spot that burns on hot soup and tingles on pineapple.

    What it teaches

    Oral-motor control (up, out, side to side — the tongue workout), taste awareness as one of the five senses, speech-sound practice through play, and the giggle factor that keeps a hidden body part in the vocabulary.

    Words to learn

    tonguetastelickwordspinkmuscle

    Say this to your child

    “"This is your tongue — the pink muscle inside your mouth! It tastes your food, it moves your food, and it shapes every word you say: la-la-la, feel it tap! It can peek out — bleh! — and hide back in, quick as a tortoise. The tongue is the busiest, silliest, strongest muscle you own."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and ask what is peeking out of the open mouth — the tongue! Name it, then find it in a mirror.
    2. Play the peek game: tongue out, tongue in, tongue up to the nose, tongue side to side. Four directions, four giggles — the tongue workout.
    3. Name the jobs: it tastes the food, moves the food for the teeth, and shapes the words. Say la-la-la and tip-tap the tongue behind the top teeth.
    4. Try the lick test: lick your lips like something yummy just happened. Then stick the tongue out for the wind to dry — that is how dogs do it.
    5. Finish with the manners: the tongue peeks for games and stays in for eating and talking. Peek now… and back in it goes, like a tortoise into its shell.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look at the picture together: what is sticking out of the open mouth? What word sits with the picture? Is the tongue out or hidden? Can you make your own do the same thing?

    Ask your child

    "Where does your tongue live?" "What does it taste — name the flavours it knows!" "What sound does la-la-la make with the tongue?" "When does the tongue peek out — and when does it stay in?"

    What your child can say or do

    Your child may run the four-direction tongue workout in the car mirror, report that llama and lollipop come from the same place, or peek the tongue and vanish it with tortoise speed — the show-off muscle, fully rehearsed.

    Out in the real world

    Tongues work at every meal and every sentence: stirring soup, checking for loose teeth, rolling Rs, licking an ice cream on a hot day. The dentist asks for it too — lift the tongue, says the mirror — and now your child knows exactly which part that is.

    Try it together

    Tongue aerobics: out-and-in for ten, up-to-the-nose for five, side-to-side for ten, then the big finish — can the tongue touch the chin? Points for trying. It is the oral-motor workout that speech therapists charge for, delivered as a comedy routine.

    Understanding check

    Ask: "Where does the tongue live? Name its jobs. Show me up, out and side to side." The mouth, the three jobs and the workout — that is the lesson landed.

    Parent tips

    The tongue workout doubles as speech practice for tricky sounds — L, T, D all live there — so keep the aerobics playful and short. And if the peeking outlasts the game, the tortoise rule is your friend: the tongue goes back in its shell for eating and talking.

    Staying safe

    The tongue stays in its own mouth — no licking friends, pets or shopping trolleys, and no touching it with fingers or toys. Hot food burns tongues first: the blowing-before-tasting rule applies here most of all, and very cold treats bite their own warning.

    This lesson pairs with the Tongue flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Body Parts & Five Senses Flashcards.

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · BODY PARTS & FIVE SENSES FLASHCARDS · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Touch — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson gives the fifth sense its doing-word. Skin does all the feeling, and touch is the word for it in action — and the card slows everything right down: one hand, laid on something soft and blue, taking its time.

    What is this?

    Touch is what skin does: it reaches out and reports what the world feels like — soft, smooth, bumpy, warm, cool, squishy. It is the fifth of the five senses, and the only one the whole body carries: hands, cheeks, toes — wherever skin goes, touch goes too.

    What does it mean?

    Touch is the sense of doing: the other four mostly take in, but touch has to reach out and meet the world first. That meeting is how babies learned everything at the start, and it is still how three-year-olds check a claim — one hand on it says more than ten words about it.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs to know: we touch with our skin, touching is the fifth sense, the hands are its best tools — and gentle is the rule: slow hands, soft landings, while hot or sharp things are for looking at and naming, not touching.

    Why this matters

    Naming touch turns feeling into vocabulary — the rug is soft, the orange is bumpy, the window is cool — and those texture words power preschool talk. It is also where gentle hands get trained: a child who can name the sense can practise the manners that come with it.

    What it teaches

    Tactile words (soft, smooth, bumpy, warm, cool), the fifth-sense framework (touch as skin’s job), gentle-hands self-regulation, slow deliberate reaching instead of grabbing, and texture discrimination through the fingers.

    Words to learn

    touchskinsoftsmoothbumpygentle

    Say this to your child

    “"Touch! Your skin is the feeler — it tells you soft, smooth, bumpy, warm, cool. Reach out slowly, land gently, and hear what your hands find. Some things we touch, and some things — hot and sharp ones — we only look at and name. Show me your gentlest touch!"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and slow everything down: what is the hand doing — resting, gently, on something soft? That careful landing is the whole lesson: touch.
    2. Name the tool: skin does the feeling, and the hands are its busiest workers. Press a palm flat on the table, then on a cushion — two reports, one sense.
    3. Play the texture hunt: find one soft thing, one smooth thing, one bumpy thing in the room. Touch each slowly and say its word out loud.
    4. Practise the gentle rule: reach out slowly, land like a butterfly, no grabbing. Try it on a teddy, on your own arm, on the rug.
    5. Set the boundary kindly: touch means gentle, and some things say look-don’t-touch — radiators, scissors, the stove. Those get pointed at and named, never handled.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look at the picture together: what is the hand doing — resting or grabbing? What color is the thing under the hand — blue? Does the hand look gentle or fast? Where does the word touch sit?

    Ask your child

    "What do we touch with?" "Which sense is touch — the fifth of how many?" "What is the softest thing in this room?" "What things in our house are look-don’t-touch?"

    What your child can say or do

    Your child may spend an afternoon patting the furniture and filing reports — bumpy, smooth, fluffy — land butterfly hands on every head in the family, or point at the stove and recite the look-don’t-touch list, finger and all.

    Out in the real world

    Touch reports arrive all day: the bumpy wall on the stairs, the smooth apple, the cold tap, the soft towel. Name what the skin sent — your hands found it! — and the fifth sense becomes a vocabulary your child uses without being asked.

    Try it together

    Mystery bag: hide three household objects — a spoon, a sponge, a small ball — inside a pillowcase. One hand in, no peeking: read it, guess, pull it out, check. Swap the cast daily. It is touch discrimination, patience and naming practice in one old sock.

    Understanding check

    Ask: "What does the skin do? Which sense number is touch? Show me a gentle landing." The feeling, the fifth and a butterfly hand — that is the lesson landed.

    Parent tips

    Keep the texture hunt to three objects a day — three good words beat ten rushed ones. And narrate your own gentle touches out loud — patting the cat, smoothing the duvet — because children copy the hands they watch, not the hands they are told about.

    Staying safe

    Touch has a look-don’t-touch list and it is real: hot oven doors, radiators, irons, scissors, knives and broken glass get pointed at and named, not handled. Gentle hands with pets and babies too — slow landings, no squeezing — and a grown-up for anything unknown.

    This lesson pairs with the Touch flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Body Parts & Five Senses Flashcards.

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · BODY PARTS & FIVE SENSES FLASHCARDS · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Taste — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson is the snack-time sense. Taste lives on the tongue, and the card catches it in action: mouth open, tongue out, a lollipop mid-test. Of all the five senses this is the one with a menu — and the best snacks for practising it.

    What is this?

    Taste is what the tongue does: it checks every bite and reports the flavour — sweet, salty, sour, bitter and yummy-all-over. It is the fourth of the five senses, and it never works alone: the nose smells every bite too, which is why food goes quiet when a blocked nose arrives.

    What does it mean?

    Taste is the safest sense to train, because the laboratory is the kitchen and the equipment is lunch. The tongue carries thousands of taste-spotters, and the nose does the fine detail — hold your nose mid-bite and everything goes mysterious. Together they turn eating into science, three times a day.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs to know: we taste with our tongue, tasting is the fourth sense, flavours have names — sweet, salty, sour — and taste has rules: only food, only with a grown-up’s okay; hot things wait until a grown-up has checked them.

    Why this matters

    A named sense gets used on purpose. Children who can say sweet and sour describe their world, try new foods as a game instead of a battle, and carry the rule that keeps the sense safe: the tongue tastes food — and only food — when a grown-up has said yes.

    What it teaches

    Flavour vocabulary (sweet, salty, sour, yum), the five-senses framework (taste as the fourth), taste-and-smell teamwork awareness, trying new foods through game framing, and the food-only rule that keeps little mouths safe.

    Words to learn

    tastetonguesweetsaltysouryum

    Say this to your child

    “"Taste! Your tongue knows flavours — sweet like banana, salty like crackers, sour like apple, yum like everything. Tasting is one of your five senses, number four! And it has rules: food only, grown-up first, and hot things get checked and blown before the tongue says hello. Ready to be a taste scientist?"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and ask what is going on — a lollipop test, tongue out, mid-taste! Name it: taste, the fourth of the five senses.
    2. Find the taste-spotters: the tongue lives in the mouth and checks every bite. Say ahh and spot it in a mirror — the pink floor where flavour lands.
    3. Play the three-flavour game at snack time: a slice of banana (sweet), a cracker (salty), a squeeze of apple (sour). One small bite each, one word each.
    4. Show the teamwork: hold your nose while tasting — suddenly everything is mysterious. Nose and tongue are a team, and food tastes bigger when both report.
    5. Set the rules with a smile: the tongue tastes food and only food, a grown-up says when it is tasting time, and hot things wait until a grown-up has checked them. Blow first, then taste.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look at the picture together: what is being tasted — a lollipop? Is the tongue out or in? What word sits with the picture? Has your child ever given a lollipop the full taste test?

    Ask your child

    "What do we taste with?" "Which sense is taste — the fourth of how many?" "What did you taste today that was sweet? Sour?" "What is the rule for hot food?"

    What your child can say or do

    Your child may grade every meal by flavour — sweet winner, sour surprise — hold a nose closed mid-dinner to prove the teamwork, or announce the rules at the table: food only, grown-up first, blow before taste.

    Out in the real world

    Taste runs through every day: the sweet bite of porridge with honey, salty lips after the pool, the sour pucker at a lemon, the yum at the end of a birthday cake. Give each flavour its word at the table and the sense becomes family vocabulary.

    Try it together

    The taste-test station: three tiny cups with a drop or crumb in each — sweet, salty, sour — eyes shut, one taste each, guess which is which. Then swap roles: your child sets the cups and quizzes you. Being the scientist is half the learning.

    Understanding check

    Ask: "What do we taste with? Name the flavours. What is the rule for hot things?" The tongue, the three words and the blow-first answer — that is the lesson landed.

    Parent tips

    Keep the tastes tiny — one crumb, one drop — and let your child spit out anything they dislike without a fuss; brave tasting grows where there is no pressure. Sour is the crowd-pleaser: one lemon face earns a whole week of requests.

    Staying safe

    Taste is the one sense that comes with a grown-up on duty: grown-ups wash the food and cut it into safe pieces, only food goes on the tongue, and hot things — soup, toast, cocoa — wait until a grown-up checks the temperature and says blow-then-taste. Anything off the floor, out of a pocket or off a plant is not food, whatever it looks like.

    This lesson pairs with the Taste flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Body Parts & Five Senses Flashcards.

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · BODY PARTS & FIVE SENSES FLASHCARDS · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Hair — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson climbs to the top of the head. Hair is the body part your child meets most often without naming it — brushed, washed, trimmed and ruffled daily — and the card gives it a face: a boy with a dark crop, ready for the pat test.

    What is this?

    Hair is the stuff that grows from the skin on top of the head — and only there, which is what gives it an address. It can be dark or light, curly or straight, long or short, thick or fine. It keeps warm the head it lives on, and it is one of the first things people notice about each other.

    What does it mean?

    Hair is the body part that is never hidden and never the same: every child in the classroom owns a different version. That makes it the gentlest possible first conversation about differences — my hair, your hair, her curls, his crop — and the easiest place to practise the big idea that different is normal.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs to know: hair grows on top of the head, out of the skin, and it comes in every colour and curl — straight, curly, dark, fair, long, short. It needs a little care: brush and wash, and a grown-up for trims. Everyone’s hair is different, and everyone’s is good.

    Why this matters

    Naming hair gives your child the word for a daily routine — the brush, the wash, the hat — and for the noticing they already do. Hair is also where children first meet difference and sameness side by side: comparing hair kindly is a small daily rehearsal for a much bigger skill.

    What it teaches

    Body-part naming above the face line, descriptive vocabulary (colour, curl, length, texture), comparing and contrasting as early thinking, gentle hands in hair-care routines, and the first friendly chat about how people differ.

    Words to learn

    hairbrushcurlsstraighttrimdark

    Say this to your child

    “"This is hair — it grows on top of your head! Yours is yours, and everyone’s is different: curly, straight, dark, fair, long, short. Hair gets brushed in the morning, washed at bath time, and trimmed by a grown-up when it gets long. Give yours a pat — is it soft? Whose hair in this family curls?"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and spot the hair: dark, drawn neatly over the boy’s head. Then find your child’s hair — same address, different style.
    2. Pat test: pat your own hair, pat your child’s — soft? fuzzy? smooth? Hair answers differently on every head, and the patting is the point.
    3. Play the mirror game: brush it smooth, ruffle it wild, spike it up, sweep it over one eye and giggle. Hair does both — tidy and wild — and so does the day.
    4. Compare kindly: whose hair in the family is curly? Whose is straight? Who has dark and who has fair? Every answer is right, and every difference is interesting.
    5. Finish with care: the brush visits every morning, the wash happens at bath time, and trims are a grown-up’s job — scissors and heads only ever meet at the barber’s.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look at the picture together: whose head is this — a boy’s? What color is his hair? Is it dark or light? What word sits with the picture? How is your own hair the same and different?

    Ask your child

    "Where does hair grow?" "What does your hair feel like — soft? curly? spiky?" "Who in our family has the curliest hair? The darkest?" "Who cuts hair when it gets long?"

    What your child can say or do

    Your child may compare hair at every opportunity — the postman’s, the dog’s, the teddy’s — report the brush results each morning, or announce that everyone’s hair is different and everyone’s is good, both parts word for word.

    Out in the real world

    Hair comes up all day: hats on and off, wind at the park, bath-night washes, the haircut chair with its cape and scissors. Name the routine — brush, wash, trim — and the morning hair battle gets a body-part reason attached.

    Try it together

    The hair salon: set up a chair, a towel cape, a soft brush and a mirror, and let your child style every teddy and doll in the house — brush, pat, announce, repeat. Then swap: your child is the barber, you are the customer, and the gentle-hands practice goes both ways.

    Understanding check

    Ask: "What grows on top of your head? What does the brush do? Who does the trims?" The place, the routine and the grown-up answer — that is the lesson landed.

    Parent tips

    Keep comparisons kind and specific — curly like grandpa, red like the neighbour — because hair is where children rehearse their first difference-talk. And let your child hold the brush even if the result is wild: a hand that brushes its own hair is a hand learning self-care.

    Staying safe

    Hair care has sharp edges: scissors and clippers are grown-up tools, and trims happen at the barber’s or with a still, sitting child and steady hands. Small clips and bobbles stay away from babies, and brushing starts at the ends and works up — gentle, not tugging.

    This lesson pairs with the Hair flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Body Parts & Five Senses Flashcards.

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · BODY PARTS & FIVE SENSES FLASHCARDS · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Chin — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson finds the smallest body part on the card — and the trickiest one to point at. The chin hides below the mouth, stars in every thinking pose, and the card settles the where-is-it question with an arrow aimed exactly at the right spot.

    What is this?

    The chin is the little bony ledge at the very bottom of the face, just under the mouth and the lips. It is what rests on a hand in a thinking pose, what tucks down when a jumper is pulled over a head, and what juts out when someone decides to be brave.

    What does it mean?

    The chin is a landmark more than a worker: the face has a map, and the chin is its bottom edge. Knowing it completes the map — forehead, eyes, nose, mouth, chin — and gives your child words for the way feelings show: chin up for brave, chin tucked for shy, chin on a hand for thinking hard.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs to know: the chin is the bony bit at the bottom of the face, just under the lips, found by tucking a finger under it — not the neck, not the cheek — and it moves with feelings: up for brave, down for thinking. Most children point at the neck first, which is what the arrow on the card is for.

    Why this matters

    The chin is usually the last face part to be named, and naming it finishes the face map. It also carries real language — chin up, chin rest, chin strap — and the finder’s pride is real, because a part this small, found this precisely, is a genuine achievement for a three-year-old finger.

    What it teaches

    Face-map completion (forehead to chin), spatial language (under, below, bottom edge), precision pointing as fine-motor practice, feeling-words linked to chin poses, and the mirror work that builds self-recognition.

    Words to learn

    chinfacearrowthinktuckunder

    Say this to your child

    “"This is your chin — the very bottom of your face, just under your lips! Tuck a finger under it: there! It is where big thoughts happen — finger on chin, hmmmm — and where brave happens too: chin up! Forehead, eyes, nose, mouth, chin: your whole face, mapped from top to bottom!"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and follow the arrow with one finger: where does it land? At the very bottom of the face — the chin. Name it, then hunt it down in a mirror.
    2. Play the finder: tuck a finger under your child’s chin — there it is! Watch out for the neck trick: the chin sits above that, just under the lip.
    3. Strike the thinker pose: finger on chin, eyebrows down, hmmmmm. Big thoughts need a chin, and the sillier the pose the better it sticks.
    4. Do the chin feelings: chin up — brave! Chin tucked — sneaky! Chin resting on both hands — bored, or thinking about snacks. Your child guesses each one.
    5. Complete the face map together: forehead, eyes, nose, mouth, chin — bottom of the map reached. Tap each one in order, faster and faster.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look at the picture together: where is the arrow pointing — at the chin? Whose face is it? Is the chin at the top of the face or the bottom? Can you find your own chin without a mirror?

    Ask your child

    "Where is your chin — show me with one finger!" "What does the chin rest on in a thinking pose?" "Which face part sits just above the chin?" "How does a brave chin stand?"

    What your child can say or do

    Your child may answer every question from here on in the thinker pose, correct a sibling who points at the neck — no, the chin, the arrow says so — or march the face map at top speed: forehead, eyes, nose, mouth, chin!

    Out in the real world

    Chins come up at the dentist — lift the chin for me — in the jumper tug when a head gets stuck halfway, and in every chins-up at the doctor’s. The face map ends at the chin, and now your child knows the last stop.

    Try it together

    Chin-and-balance races: walk a line on the floor with a soft toy balanced on the chin — wobbling allowed, giggling guaranteed. Or pass a balloon chin-to-chin with a partner: no hands, chins only. It is chin awareness, posture control and comedy in one game.

    Understanding check

    Ask: "Where is the chin? What sits just above it? Show me the thinker pose." The bottom-of-the-face answer, the lips and a thoughtful hmm — that is the lesson landed.

    Parent tips

    If the finger keeps landing on the neck, go back to the mirror and trace the jaw together — bottom of the face, under the lips, a small bony ledge. And let the thinker pose become a family joke: a child who strikes it mid-conversation is a child who owns the word.

    Staying safe

    Chins take the fall in trips — they land first when feet race wheels — so every chin bump gets a grown-up’s look, a cold cloth and a cuddle. Helmet chin straps get buckled before wheels roll: the strap lives under the chin, and so does the rule — helmet on, strap clicked, then ride.

    This lesson pairs with the Chin flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Body Parts & Five Senses Flashcards.

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · BODY PARTS & FIVE SENSES FLASHCARDS · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Cheeks — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson lands on the softest part of the face. Cheeks sit below the eyes and beside the smile; they puff, blush and hold kisses — and the card catches them at their best: rosy, round and grinning.

    What is this?

    The cheeks are the two soft round parts of the face, below the eyes and either side of the mouth. They puff out for blowing, lift high for a real smile, go rosy in the cold and hold still for kisses. Everyone has two, and no two pairs match.

    What does it mean?

    Cheeks are the face’s weather report and its mood ring: pink in the cold, flushed after running, puffed mid-bubble, dimpled mid-giggle. They are also the place people reach for first — a kiss lands there, a gentle pat calms there — which makes them the face’s comfort corner.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs to know: cheeks are the soft parts either side of the smile, they puff like balloons for blowing, they show pink in cold weather and after running, and gentle pats and kisses land on them. Cheeks get gentle hands: no pinching, no squeezing.

    Why this matters

    Cheek words carry feelings — rosy, puffed, dimpled — and cold-weather talk: hat on, cheeks pink. Naming them gives your child the vocabulary for how a face shows what it feels, and the pat-pat game doubles as a calm-down trick that works on wobbly days.

    What it teaches

    Face-map vocabulary below the eyes, descriptive feeling-words (rosy, puffed, dimpled), oral-motor play through cheek puffing, gentle-touch practice, and the soothing ritual of the calm pat.

    Words to learn

    cheeksrosypuffpatsmilepink

    Say this to your child

    “"These are your cheeks — one here, one here, soft as pillows! They puff up like balloons — pfff — they go pink in the cold, they lift up when you smile, and they catch kisses. Pat them gently, pat-pat. Can you puff them up big? Now let the air out — pbbbbfft!"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and find the cheeks: two soft rounds, one on each side of the smile. Then find your child’s — count them: one, two.
    2. Pat gently, both of you: pat-pat, like a tiny drum on dough. Gentle is the rule — cheeks are for soft pats, not pinches.
    3. Play the balloon game: puff both cheeks up full, then let the air out with a pbbbbfft. Try holding the puff while the other counts — three seconds is the record attempt.
    4. Test the weather report: puff and blow — cheeks working. Pretend to shiver — cheeks going pink. Big smile — cheeks lifting high. The face talks with its cheeks.
    5. Finish with the landing: where do grandma kisses arrive? On the cheeks! One kiss, one pat, and the cheeks are officially the family’s comfort corner.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look at the picture together: is the face smiling? What color are the cheeks — rosy? How many cheeks can you count? What word sits with the picture? Can you puff your own like balloons?

    Ask your child

    "Where are your cheeks — show me both!" "What do cheeks do when we blow? When we smile?" "What color do cheeks go in the cold?" "Who lands kisses on your cheeks?"

    What your child can say or do

    Your child may patrol the family for cheek-patting rights — gently, gently — puff on demand and deflate with full sound effects, or report the weather on every face: pink cheeks, cold day, hat needed.

    Out in the real world

    Cheeks report all day: rosy after the slide, pink at the bus stop, puffed over a bowl of bubble mix, lifted at the door when you come home. Name the report — your cheeks say you had fun — and the face gains a weather channel.

    Try it together

    The cheek orchestra: everyone puffs at the count of three, holds for two, and deflates on the conductor’s signal — louder, longer, higher on request. Then the slow movement: gentle pat-pat on your own cheeks, softer and softer until the hands rest. It is breath control disguised as a brass section.

    Understanding check

    Ask: "Where are the cheeks? What do they do when we blow? How do we touch them — gently or pinchy?" The pair, the puff and the gentle answer — that is the lesson landed.

    Parent tips

    The slow pat-pat is a real calming tool on wobbly days — softer, slower, quieter until the storm passes; children borrow the calm from the rhythm. And let blowing practice live here too: puffed cheeks are the first step toward candles, whistles and bubbles.

    Staying safe

    Cheeks are for gentle: no pinching, no squeezing, no grabbing faces, however cute the moment — the rule is said kindly and often. Cold, windy days chap little cheeks, so hats, scarves and a dab of cream do the guarding, and very sore or swollen cheeks get a grown-up’s check.

    This lesson pairs with the Cheeks flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Body Parts & Five Senses Flashcards.

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · BODY PARTS & FIVE SENSES FLASHCARDS · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Look — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson puts the eyes to work. See is the sense; look is the job — bending down, getting close, taking your time. The card shows it exactly: a boy folded low over a red ball, close enough to study every inch of it.

    What is this?

    Look is what eyes do on purpose: point them at something and study it. Looking is slower than seeing — the whole body helps, bending down, holding still, getting close. It is the eyes’ doing-word, and it is the difference between a glance and a real investigation.

    What does it mean?

    See happens whether you choose it or not; look is the chosen version — attention aimed on purpose. That aiming is the first scientific skill your child owns: freeze, focus, study, report. The card’s bent knees say it plainly: looking closely is body work, and it takes practise.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs to know: we look with our eyes, looking means slowing down and getting close — bend, freeze, study — it is the doing-word for the seeing sense, and moving feet get eyes up: eyes study best when the body is still, so feet stop first, then eyes work.

    Why this matters

    Look is one of the most-used words in a preschool day — look at this, look where you are going, look at me! — and a child who owns the word owns the game of noticing. Looking closely feeds every later skill: puzzles, books, patterns, science, and the find-your-shoes speed run at the door.

    What it teaches

    Visual attention and deliberate focus, body-stillness as a condition for looking, action-word (verb) vocabulary, near-and-far looking ranges, and observation as the first step of the science habit.

    Words to learn

    lookeyesclosestudyspotfreeze

    Say this to your child

    “"Look! Your eyes have a doing-word, and this is it: look. Bend down slow, hold still, and really study something — a red ball, a bug, a pattern. What did the long look find that the quick one missed? And remember: feet stop first, then eyes work. Show me your best freeze-and-look!"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card: what is the boy doing — bending down, low and slow, to look at something? And at what? A red ball, worth studying.
    2. Copy the pose: bend down low together and pick one thing to study — a toy, a shell, a pattern on the rug. Ten slow seconds, then report: what did the close look find?
    3. Play look-up-look-down: look up high, look down low, look behind you, look between your knees. Freeze after each one — looking bodies are still bodies.
    4. Try near and far: hold a toy at nose distance and study it, then set it across the room and study it again. Same toy, two reports — looking has ranges.
    5. Set the feet rule: when feet are moving, eyes go up; when eyes want to study, feet stop first. Look while still, walk while watching — that is the safe way round.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look at the picture together: what is the boy doing — bending down? What is he studying — a red ball? Is he up close or far off? What word sits with the picture? What was the last thing you bent down to look at?

    Ask your child

    "What do we look with?" "How is looking different from just seeing?" "Show me a freeze-and-look — what did you find?" "What is the rule for feet and eyes when we walk?"

    What your child can say or do

    Your child may drop into the freeze-and-look pose mid-pavement — ladybug under study, feet already stopped — issue look! commands at every window, or explain the feet rule to a running friend: stop first, then eyes.

    Out in the real world

    Look runs the whole day: look both ways at the kerb, look for the missing shoe, look at this drawing, look how tall the tower got. Each command lands better on a child who knows that looking is a skill — and that feet stop before eyes start.

    Try it together

    The close-study gallery: collect three small treasures — a pinecone, a shell, a big leaf — and give each a full slow look, ten seconds minimum, then a report of three findings. Line them up on a shelf as the gallery. Fresh treasures weekly; the study habit grows with the collection.

    Understanding check

    Ask: "What do we look with? Show me a freeze-and-look. What do feet do first?" The eyes, the pose and the stop answer — that is the lesson landed.

    Parent tips

    Give the study time room to be slow — the whole point is the long look, and three-year-olds need seconds to find the details. And join in: study one thing yourself and report out loud, because a child who watches a grown-up look closely learns what close looking looks like.

    Staying safe

    Looking has a moving-feet rule: no studying while walking — feet stop, then eyes work — or kerbs and table corners collect their toll. And the sun rule holds here too: eyes never study the sun, whatever the game — hats and shade do the guarding on bright days.

    This lesson pairs with the Look flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Body Parts & Five Senses Flashcards.

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · BODY PARTS & FIVE SENSES FLASHCARDS · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Listen — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson turns the ears into detectives. Hear is the sense; listen is the decision to use it on purpose — and the card shows the trade’s oldest trick: a hand cupped behind an ear, gathering every sound in the room.

    What is this?

    Listen is what ears do on purpose: shut out the busy stuff and focus on one sound. The cupped hand behind the ear helps — it gathers sound like a little satellite dish. Listening is hearing with attention added, and it needs a still body to work best.

    What does it mean?

    Hear is automatic; listen is chosen. The cupped hand makes the choice visible — a pose the whole world reads as paying attention. That pose is worth teaching: it turns waiting into an action, gives fidgety hands a job, and makes a three-year-old’s listening look as serious as it feels.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs to know: we listen with our ears, listening is hearing with attention — still body, cupped hands if wanted — listening works best when the body holds still, whispers are the best listening practice, and a good listener is a treasure at story time, music time and road-crossing time.

    Why this matters

    Listening is the classroom skill hiding inside a game: stories, instructions, music and friendship all run on it. Naming listen gives the pose a word, the stillness a reason and the whisper games a purpose — and a child who can listen on request carries the skill straight into circle time.

    What it teaches

    Auditory attention and focus, the hear-listen distinction (automatic versus chosen), body-stillness and impulse control, whisper-voice play, and the cupped-ear pose as visible attention for group settings.

    Words to learn

    listenearcupwhisperstillsound

    Say this to your child

    “"Listen! Your ears have a doing-word too: listen. Cup your hand behind your ear — see, it gathers the sound in! Listening works best when bodies hold still, so feet stop, hands cup, and we catch the sound: my whisper, the clock, a bird outside. What can your cupped ears find right now?"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and copy the pose: hand cupped behind the ear. What is the boy doing — listening hard! The cup makes the ears bigger and the listening official.
    2. Try the cup test: listen to the room with hands down, then hands cupped behind both ears. Louder? Different? The dish trick is real.
    3. Play the whisper game: send one whispered word across the room — cup the ear, lean in, catch it. Then swap: your child whispers, you listen.
    4. Prove the stillness rule: stomp once, then freeze — a listening body is a still body. Try listening while wiggling, then while frozen. Frozen wins every time.
    5. Go on a sound hunt: sit still for one minute, a finger up for each sound caught — clock, fridge, birds, a door somewhere. Compare catches at the end.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look at the picture together: where is the boy’s hand — cupped behind his ear? Which ear? Is he standing still? What word sits with the picture? Can you make the same listening pose?

    Ask your child

    "What do we listen with?" "What does the cupped hand do?" "Show me a listening body — what do the feet do?" "What did your cupped ears catch today?"

    What your child can say or do

    Your child may adopt the cupped-ear pose for every story from here on, whisper everything for a day — secret word included — or freeze mid-game, hand to ear, and announce the post van two streets away before anyone else hears it.

    Out in the real world

    Listen is a daily instruction: listen to the kettle, listen for the timer, listen to grandma’s story, listen at the road. Each one works better on a child who owns the pose and the stillness — and the road one is the reason the practice matters.

    Try it together

    Sound catchers: everyone cups their ears and shuts their eyes for one minute, raising a finger for each sound caught, then compares lists — the fridge, the washing machine, a dog, a chair creak. Play it outdoors for bigger catches. Stillness with a mission is the whole trick.

    Understanding check

    Ask: "What do we listen with? What does the cupped hand do? What do listening bodies hold?" The ears, the dish and the still answer — that is the lesson landed.

    Parent tips

    Make the cupped-ear pose your signal at story time — hand up, ears cupped, room settles — because a pose works faster than a shout. And keep whispers precious: a voice that only whispers for secrets gets the best listening in the house.

    Staying safe

    Listening practice has a safety catch: the still-body rule matters most at the road — stop, look and listen is the crossing rhyme, and it works with a grown-up holding hands. Ears stay delicate too: no shouting into cupped ears, even for fun, and loud sounds get stepped away from.

    This lesson pairs with the Listen flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Body Parts & Five Senses Flashcards.

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · BODY PARTS & FIVE SENSES FLASHCARDS · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Feel — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson sends the skin to work. Touch is the sense; feel is the doing-word — and the card keeps it gentle: one hand, moving slowly, reading something soft and white like a story written in texture.

    What is this?

    Feel is what skin does when it pays attention: a hand settles on something and reads it — soft, smooth, warm, squishy, bumpy. It is the doing-word for the touch sense, and the word wears two hats in your house: I feel the blanket and I feel happy share one useful verb.

    What does it mean?

    Feel is the slow version of touch — not a grab, a read. The hand moves, the brain collects, the word arrives: soft. And the same verb carries feelings, which is a quiet piece of luck: a child who can say I feel the blanket is one step from saying I feel sad, and both sentences deserve the same listening.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs to know: we feel with our skin, feeling means slow and careful — a hand that reads, not a hand that grabs — textures have names: soft, smooth, bumpy, warm, squishy — and feel talks about textures and feelings both: I feel the teddy, I feel happy.

    Why this matters

    Feel is a two-for-one word: texture vocabulary and emotion vocabulary share it. Practising the texture side — blanket, sponge, spoon — builds the describing words preschool runs on, and the feeling side gives your child a ready-made way to name the inside weather: I feel happy, I feel cross, I feel cosy.

    What it teaches

    Tactile discrimination and texture vocabulary, the touch-feel verb link, emotional naming through the shared word feel, slow deliberate hand movement (reading, not grabbing), and comparison skills across textures.

    Words to learn

    feelhandsoftsmoothsquishycosy

    Say this to your child

    “"Feel! Your skin has a doing-word: feel. Put your hand down slow — like this — and read it: soft, smooth, warm, squishy. And feel has two jobs: I feel the soft blanket, and I feel happy — same word! Slow hands read best, and new things get a grown-up check first. What does this cushion feel like?"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card: what is the hand doing — reading something soft with slow fingers? That careful reading is called feeling.
    2. Copy the hand: settle your palm on a cushion, shut your eyes, and read it — soft? squishy? warm? Fingertips first, slow as syrup.
    3. Build the texture corner: a blanket, one spoon and a sponge side by side. Feel each with eyes shut and say its word — soft, cold and smooth, squishy.
    4. Play the two-hats game: I feel the blanket — texture! I feel happy — feeling! Same word, two jobs. Make three sentences each and giggle at the crossover.
    5. Set the care rule: feeling hands go slow, and unknown things get a grown-up check first — radiators and bath water are for grown-ups to test, hands to confirm.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look at the picture together: what is happening — a hand reading something soft and white? Does the touch look slow or quick? What word sits with the picture? What did your fingers read today?

    Ask your child

    "What do we feel with?" "What did your hand feel today — soft? bumpy? warm?" "How does a feeling hand move — fast or slow?" "Say one sentence about a texture and one about a feeling!"

    What your child can say or do

    Your child may run a fingertip along every wall and cushion in the house, filing reports — bumpy, smooth, cosy — declare I feel happy, I feel the teddy, I feel lunch, or test the two-hats rule on a grandparent for confirmation.

    Out in the real world

    Feel works everywhere: the warm bath tested with a toe, the soft jumper pulled close, the cold spoon at breakfast, the squashy sponge at sink time. Name what the hand read — your fingers felt it first — and the doing-word earns its keep twice a day.

    Try it together

    Texture lucky dip: a pillowcase hiding a wooden block, a scrunch of foil and a soft toy. One hand in, eyes shut: read the mystery with fingertips, guess, then pull it out to check. Swap the cast daily. Fingertip reading is the game; texture vocabulary is the prize.

    Understanding check

    Ask: "What do we feel with? How does a feeling hand move? Name two textures you read today." The skin, the slowness and the words — that is the lesson landed.

    Parent tips

    Keep the texture corner to three objects and rotate weekly — three words done well beat ten rushed. And honour the second hat: when your child says I feel sad or I feel happy, treat it as the same skill practised — naming, exactly like the blanket got named.

    Staying safe

    Feeling hands get a check-first rule: radiators, bath water, oven doors and anything hot or unknown are tested by a grown-up first, then confirmed by careful fingers. Gentle is the touch — no squeezing pets, no prodding babies — and anything sharp or breakable stays on the look-only shelf.

    This lesson pairs with the Feel flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Body Parts & Five Senses Flashcards.
